source.title: Generalization Bounds for Neural Belief Propagation Decoders
source.authors: S. Adiga; Xin Xiao; Ravi Tandon; B. Vasic; Tamal Bose

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper, including appendices; no material cut-off or garbling noted.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures train–test BER gaps in neural belief propagation decoders and varies training-set size, decoding iterations, codeword length, and channel noise. These results bear on generalization-gap conditions but do not test the specific behaviors in V1–V8.
record.gate_note: Rows capture the paper’s own empirical gap results. Theoretical bounds, cited prior-work findings, and figure values not described in the text are not recorded as separate results.
record.test_reason: The study derives bounds and measures train–test bit-error-rate gaps for neural belief propagation decoders. Its dataset-size, depth, noise and blocklength sweeps test none of V1–V8. Using Adam without an optimizer comparison does not test V4; discussing perturbation-based bounds does not test V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's empirical paraphrase is accurate, with blocklength results specifically measured using gaps normalized by training BER. The authors also emphasize their theoretical bounds for regular and irregular parity-check matrices and extensions accounting for channel characteristics. They interpret the empirical size, iteration and blocklength trends as consistent with these bounds.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses NBP decoders for noisy linear-code decoding, trained with Adam on cross-entropy; it does not reproduce the memorization, optimizer, batch, dropout, sharpness, or example-removal methods in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: The measured gap varies with training dataset size, decoding iterations, Gaussian noise standard deviation, and blocklength. The authors also state the inverse dataset-size trend was consistent across tested T and SNR values, and the iteration trend across dataset sizes and SNR values; plots for the former are omitted.

fits_no_version.finding: For the tested Tanner-code decoders, the BER gap generally decreases as training-set size increases from 1,000 to 10,000.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing training-set size generally reduces the generalization gap of the tested NBP decoders.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors report that the BER gap grows linearly with decoding iterations from 2 to 10.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing decoding depth increases the generalization gap of the tested NBP decoders.

fits_no_version.finding: The gap increases up to approximately β = 1 and then decreases; large noise raises both training and test BER.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Channel noise changes NBP generalization gaps non-monotonically, and a smaller gap can accompany worse decoding performance.

fits_no_version.finding: The gap normalized by training BER increases with blocklength within the tested QC-LDPC families, while code rate also changes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Normalized NBP generalization gaps increase with blocklength in the tested code families under their accompanying code-rate changes.

record.problems: The experiments cover NBP decoders and specific code/channel settings, not the claim versions’ architectures or interventions. Experimental results are summarized mainly by qualitative plot descriptions; exact plotted values are not stated in the text. The blocklength descendants also vary in code-rate.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Individual parameter points within the dataset-size, iteration, and blocklength sweeps are not separately transcribed because the text gives qualitative sweep-level trends and the values appear in plots.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting versus natural-label held-out performance under the same architecture and training recipe.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of learned local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer performance and dependence on tuning or optimizer adaptations.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove those effects.
Dropout interventions, underfitting, dataset-size dependence and removal with weight decay under augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness correlations with generalization gaps and comparisons against norm- and margin-based rankings.
Removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples and measuring test accuracy.

record.verdict_notes: T6 applies relative to the specified versions, despite the study's original research on generalization. All row states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8; this does not dispute the reported adjacent trends. No version-bearing results are missing.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence; the named architectures and datasets.
Width sweeps beyond interpolation and test error versus width.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizer comparisons and tuning or weight-decay conditions.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Magnitude-aware sharpness measurements and their correlation with the gap.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the test-accuracy effect.

rows.subject: NBP decoder, (155,93)-Tanner code
rows.operation_detail: Varied training dataset size from m = 103 to m = 104 in steps of 1000; measured test–training average BER gap.

conditions.value: m = 103 to m = 104 in steps of 1000

rows.measure: Generalization gap (average test BER minus training BER)
rows.value: The generalization gap is the largest for m = 1000, and generally decays with m.
rows.uncertainty: 10 trials; distribution plotted as a boxplot; numerical uncertainty not stated.
rows.note: The text reports a qualitative trend; individual figure values are not transcribed.
rows.check: The trend is accurately reported but measures no claim version. Write the dataset range as 10^3–10^4, not 103–104. The figures identify k = 93, while Section 4's opening specifies k = 64; flag the source inconsistency.

rows.note: The authors say very large β reduces the gap while raising training and test BER.
